title: Building Quantum-Ready Infrastructure: Preparing for the Physical Demands of Quantum Computing
gist: Quantum computing's scaling constraint will not be electricity but architecture-specific industrial supply chains: helium-3 and dilution refrigerators for superconducting systems, lasers, optics and ultra-high vacuum for neutral atom and trapped-ion systems. With commercialization possibly accelerating in the early 2030s, the piece argues the United States has a narrow planning window to avoid repeating AI's infrastructure lag, where data center capex is set to hit nearly $750 billion in 2026.

insights.claim: Quantum computing has no single infrastructure blueprint: superconducting and silicon spin systems strain cryogenic and helium-3 supply chains while neutral atom and trapped-ion systems strain lasers, optics and vacuum equipment.
insights.so_what: Investment exposure to quantum should be sized by architecture-specific input suppliers, not by a single generic quantum supply chain basket.
insights.quote: the binding inputs will vary by architecture, deployment pathway, and scale
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Superconducting and silicon spin architectures depend on dilution refrigerators that cool to roughly 10-20 millikelvin, making cryogenic supply chains as important as access to electricity for those systems.
insights.so_what: Cryostat manufacturers and helium-3 supply are a concentrated, under-covered pinch point if superconducting wins.
insights.quote: For these architectures, cryogenic supply chains are poised to become as important as access to electricity.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Neutral atom and trapped-ion systems generally avoid dilution refrigerators entirely, so their bottlenecks emerge in ultra-high-vacuum environments, high-power stable lasers, precision optics and optical control rather than in helium-3.
insights.so_what: A modality shift away from superconducting would reroute the entire bottleneck to photonics and vacuum vendors, a different investable set.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: An Oak Ridge National Laboratory study of six fault-tolerant superconducting quantum scenarios through 2045 examined electricity, water, nitrogen, helium and helium-3, concluding the binding constraints are cryogenic systems, helium-3 availability, cooling infrastructure and specialized manufacturing capacity rather than raw power.
insights.so_what: A named, citable source for the contrarian view that quantum is not an AI-style power story.
insights.locator: A recent study by Oak Ridge National Laboratory
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Qubit materials span elemental silicon, III-V semiconductors, diamond, aluminum and rare earth metals, with each architecture requiring different materials, fabrication processes and supply chains.
insights.so_what: Adds critical-minerals exposure to the quantum thesis and links it to existing rare-earth supply politics.
insights.locator: Quantum computing also depends on critical raw materials
insights.speaker: CSIS

themes.theme: AI buildout as the cautionary precedent

insights.claim: BloombergNEF projects capital expenditure by the world's 14 largest data center service companies to reach nearly $750 billion in 2026, up from less than $450 billion in 2025.
insights.so_what: A roughly 67 percent year-on-year capex jump is the scale benchmark against which any quantum buildout should be judged, and a live number for the AI infrastructure trade.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Seventy-five percent of U.S. data centers under construction as of September 2025 are expected to consume more than 23 gigawatts, and by 2030 peak demand is estimated to add about 84 gigawatts, the equivalent of Texas's entire electricity consumption, to a national demand that has been flat since the 1970s.
insights.so_what: Quantifies the U.S. power demand regime change, the core input for utilities, IPPs and grid equipment theses.
insights.locator: Of the data centers under construction in the United States
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Efficiency gains in AI increase rather than reduce total resource demand as lower costs unlock more use cases and queries, a Jevons Paradox dynamic that could repeat around quantum facilities, components and materials.
insights.so_what: Cheaper compute is not a bear case for infrastructure suppliers; it is the mechanism that expands their addressable demand.
insights.locator: AI also illustrates how efficiency gains
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The transferable lesson from AI is not an identical demand curve but that energy systems, permitting, capital markets and supply chains cannot adjust fast enough once demand accelerates, turning them into strategic constraints.
insights.so_what: Argues the infrastructure premium accrues to whoever builds capacity before the demand signal is obvious.
insights.quote: When demand accelerates faster than planning, energy systems, permitting processes, capital markets, and supply chains can become strategic constraints.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The supply chains, permitting pathways and capital markets supporting quantum are less mature than those behind semiconductor fabrication or data center construction today, so they would struggle to absorb a demand surge.
insights.so_what: Implies quantum scaling would bottleneck faster and at lower absolute demand than AI did.
insights.speaker: CSIS

themes.theme: Policy window and what to build now

insights.claim: Quantum commercialization may accelerate in the early 2030s while the supply chains, facilities, workforce pipelines and permitting pathways needed to support it take years to prepare.
insights.so_what: Gives a rough timing anchor for when quantum-adjacent industrial demand could inflect.
insights.locator: Because quantum computing has not yet reached AI-like scale
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Cryogenic, laser, photonics and precision optics suppliers are being pulled toward faster-growing AI markets, which is precisely where targeted incentives may be needed to preserve quantum-relevant capacity.
insights.so_what: Identifies a crowding-out mechanism: AI demand can starve quantum of its own component base, a risk for quantum hardware timelines.
insights.quote: especially where suppliers are focused on faster-growing AI markets
insights.locator: Strengthen supply chain resilience before shortages emerge
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Quantum readiness should be treated as an industrial infrastructure challenge rather than a computing challenge, requiring firms that manufacture and maintain cryostats, recycle scarce cryogenic gases, build laser and optical systems and secure high-purity materials.
insights.so_what: Reframes where quantum value accrues: toward picks-and-shovels industrial suppliers rather than processor vendors.
insights.locator: This physical stack makes quantum infrastructure
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Many current quantum projects sit on national or state-owned property where review processes are easier, so commercialization at scale would require new siting options and faster permitting frameworks for quantum facilities and cryostat manufacturing plants.
insights.so_what: Permitting reform is a concrete, watchable policy catalyst for the quantum industrial base, mirroring the AI data center permitting push.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Early quantum deployments such as Department of Energy user facilities and Quantum Genesis should be treated as data-collection platforms for real resource use, helium losses, cooling-water demand and supply delays rather than as demonstrations.
insights.so_what: Operational data from pilots is where the real constraint estimates will come from, so those disclosures are the signal to watch.
insights.locator: Use pilot facilities to collect operational data
insights.speaker: CSIS
